Patient
PAY-shent
adj.
From Latin patiens, the present participle of pati, to suffer, to endure. Webster 1828: having the quality of enduring evils without murmuring; not easily provoked; calmly waiting for something expected. The word means suffering before it means waiting.

Biblical Definition

Patient in the New Testament is a duty of every believer, a qualification for office, and a description of the farmer who has no other option. Paul lists it in his short catalogue of how a congregation deals with its own difficult members: warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all men (1 Thessalonians 5:14). Four different responses to four different people — the unruly are warned, the fainthearted comforted, the weak supported — and patience covers them all. It is required in an elder: the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient (2 Timothy 2:24), and the context is a man dealing with people who oppose themselves. James grounds the church’s patience in an event: Be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain (James 5:7) — the farmer’s patience is not resignation but confidence in a harvest he cannot hurry. And the Preacher weighs it against its opposite: Better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof: and the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit (Ecclesiastes 7:8).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines PATIENT as having the quality of enduring evils without murmuring or fretfulness; sustaining afflictions with fortitude and submission to the divine will; not easily provoked; calmly waiting for what is expected.

expand to see more

PATIENT, a. — Having the quality of enduring evils without murmuring or fretfulness.

Sustaining afflictions of body or mind with fortitude, calmness, or Christian submission to the divine will.

Not easily provoked; calm under the sufferance of injuries or offences.

Persevering; constant in pursuit or exertion; calmly diligent; and, waiting with calmness or contentment.

From Latin patior, to suffer — the root also of passion, compassion, and passive.

Key Scripture

1 Thessalonians 5:14 — "Now we exhort you, brethren, warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all men."

2 Timothy 2:24 — "And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient,"

James 5:7 — "Be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain."

Ecclesiastes 7:8 — "Better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof: and the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit."

Modern Corruption

1 Thessalonians 5:14 assigns four different treatments to four different kinds of people, and the modern pastoral instinct that applies comfort universally gives the unruly exactly what Paul says not to give them.

expand to see more

Paul’s verse is a piece of pastoral triage and the distinctions are the point. Warn them that are unruly — the word is military, of a soldier out of rank; such a man needs admonition, not sympathy. Comfort the feebleminded — literally the small-souled, the discouraged; they need consolation, not warning. Support the weak — hold them up, which implies a burden actually carried. And then, over all three, be patient toward all men. A ministry that comforts everyone will confirm the unruly in their disorder; a ministry that warns everyone will crush the fainthearted. Getting the category wrong is not a small mistake, and the same apostle who wrote this wrote that the servant of the Lord must be apt to teach, patient, in meekness instructing those that oppose themselves.

James 5:7 sets the whole matter in the only frame that makes it bearable. The farmer waits because the harvest is certain and the rains are appointed, not because waiting is a virtue in itself. Christian patience is eschatological: be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord, and James adds two verses later, the coming of the Lord draweth nigh… behold, the judge standeth before the door. Where the second coming becomes a distant abstraction, patience loses its object and turns into mere endurance or, more often, into demands for immediate resolution. Ecclesiastes 7:8 states the alternative bluntly: the patient in spirit is better than the proud, and pride is the reason most impatience exists.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek makrothumeo (G3114), to be long-tempered, to be patient; makrothumia (G3115), longsuffering; hupomone (G5281), endurance under a load; anexikakos (G420), patient of wrong.

expand to see more

Greek makrothumeo (G3114) — to be long-tempered, slow to anger; be patient toward all men (1 Thessalonians 5:14) and the farmer of James 5:7.

Greek makrothumia (G3115) — longsuffering; a fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22) and an attribute of God (Romans 2:4).

Greek hupomone (G5281) — endurance, remaining under a weight; the patience that worketh experience (Romans 5:3).

Greek anexikakos (G420) — enduring evil without resentment; the patient of 2 Timothy 2:24.

Greek ataktos (G813) — disorderly, out of rank; the unruly of 1 Thessalonians 5:14, a military term.

Usage

"Warn them that are unruly… be patient toward all men (1 Thessalonians 5:14) — four treatments, four kinds of people."

"Apt to teach, patient (2 Timothy 2:24) — required of the man who must instruct those that oppose themselves."

"The husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth (James 5:7) — patience with an object, not resignation."
